episode_title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes

stories.topic: The boss who made people cry, and why they kept coming back
stories.summary: Amit opens by passing on what a former colleague of Ajay's told him. She had worked with Ajay for four years and has spent many years at the UN. She called him a monster who often made her weep, and said this happened to everyone. Yet they all kept returning to work with him, because they learned so much and, above all, learned how to learn. Ajay answered that the most interesting things in life are invisible spillovers that no market transaction captures.
stories.insight: Demanding mentorship hurts at the time and transforms people later. Ajay frames this kind of influence as a positive externality: we are each a linear combination of our influences, and most of the good in the world happens through these unpriced spillovers.
stories.quote: He would make me cry. So often I have sat weeping in front of him. This is common for everyone, not just for me. But we always used to come back and work with him again.

stories.summary: Drawing on Gary Taubes, Amit explains that cigarette smoke was alkaline until 1913, so trying to inhale it made you cough. That year the new Camel brand raised the tobacco's carbohydrate (sugar) content. The smoke turned acidic, became easy to inhale, and became more addictive.
stories.insight: This is a hidden link between two great public-health villains. Sugar was more than a parallel addiction to tobacco; it helped make deep inhalation, and so lung cancer, possible at scale.
stories.quote: I would say that in a sense, sugars enabled smoking to cause lung cancer. Until nineteen thirteen, cigarette smoke was alkaline.

stories.topic: When experts blamed automobiles instead of sugar
stories.summary: As early as 1907, the Bengali physician Kailas Chunder Bose linked rising diabetes to growing wealth under British rule, and early physicians tied diabetes to carbohydrates. Then Elliott Joslin, America's dominant diabetes physician, looked for other causes. In 1925 he claimed automobiles cause diabetes, because people stopped walking and got fat. His ally Harold Himsworth published a now-discredited paper blaming fat. Meanwhile Prohibition pushed Americans from alcohol toward candy, and sugar consumption soared.
stories.insight: Wrong ideas take hold through institutional silos. Physicians understood hormones but not diet, nutritionists understood diet but not hormones, and nobody yet grasped insulin resistance. Once a theory took root, careers were built on it and it became self-protecting.
stories.quote: So people are coming up with other theories. Those theories take root, then cabals build along those theories, careers are based on those theories and so on and so forth.

stories.topic: Ancel Keys and the cherry-picked Seven Countries Study
stories.summary: In the late 1950s, the University of Minnesota researcher Ancel Keys published his famous Seven Countries Study blaming saturated fat for heart disease. He left out countries that could have disproved him, such as France, with its high-fat diet and low heart disease, and Switzerland and Germany. He also ignored that his chosen countries ate a lot of sugar. The American Heart Association argued against him in 1957, but by 1960 he sat on its main panel, and in 1961 it issued low-fat guidelines. Amit says obesity rose from roughly one in seven to one in three Americans over the next forty years.
stories.insight: Science advances by testing your hypothesis against the evidence most likely to break it. When an influential researcher does the opposite and captures the institutions, a whole society can follow bad advice for decades.
stories.quote: So he cherry picks the countries, then he cherry picks the evidence, then he comes to the conclusion that fat is the problem.

stories.summary: In 1976 Jean Mayer wrote a New York Times piece on the bitter truth about sugar. Reader's Digest planned to run excerpts, but after the sugar lobby phoned the managing editor, the piece was spiked. Researcher David Kritchevsky, quoted in Nina Teicholz's book, described how fiercely anyone questioning official advice was attacked. In 1977 the US Senate's Dietary Goals recommended low fat and called sugar fine. Teicholz's chart shows the American obesity curve shooting up from around that time.
stories.insight: An orthodoxy enforced by industry money and social outrage can look like settled science. Amit thinks this scandal is bigger than the tobacco lobby's.
stories.quote: We were jumped on. People would just spit on us. It's hard to imagine now the heat of the passion. It was just like we had desecrated the American flag.

stories.topic: Chandra Bhan Prasad's pride in his diabetic village elders
stories.summary: Ajay asked whether rising sugar consumption was just income elasticity. Amit agreed prosperity plays a part, but noted that Japan, France and Germany grew richer without the same outcome, so culture matters too. He then recalled the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad telling him that obese, diabetic village elders fill his heart with pride. Their grandparents could never have been prosperous enough to get diabetes. Prasad makes a similar point about the ghunghat. Lower-caste women were once barred from wearing it, so a Dalit bride wearing one is exercising a choice she was denied, even though Amit had always seen it as patriarchal oppression.
stories.insight: The same fact can mean very different things from different vantage points. What looks like a health crisis or oppression from one lens can be a marker of hard-won mobility and agency from another.
stories.quote: When I go back to my village and I see my village elders are obese and they have diabetes, my heart fills with pride.

stories.summary: Five years as a professional poker player, playing 15-hour sessions, took Amit to 105 kg. About five or six years ago he read the books, did keto plus intermittent fasting plus daily running, dropped to 85-86 kg, ran a 10k, and held that weight for a long time. COVID made him sedentary and comfort food took over, one biryani or pizza at a time, until he reached 107 kg. About 18 months before this episode he was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, with an HbA1c of 7.7. Three months on metformin changed little. Then Ajay suggested a continuous glucose monitor (CGM). A slice of toast sent him to 285, while eggs and bacon left a flat line. He moved to keto and then one meal a day, cooking two- or three-course dinners to music between six and eight, and brought his HbA1c down to 5.7.
stories.insight: Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it. Amit had already gifted The Diabetes Code to friends but was too lazy to act. Real-time feedback on his own body is what closed the gap.
stories.quote: It's just one meal. And so one meal at a time, I went in the wrong direction, went to 107.

stories.summary: After his diagnosis, Amit's doctor prescribed metformin and the usual drugs. When Amit asked about diet, the doctor looked embarrassed and said only, 'You're a smart man, you know what to do.' Ajay offered a reading of that moment: with non-communicable diseases, doctors act as amateur psychologists, judging a patient's discipline and tailoring advice to what they think the patient will actually do.
stories.insight: Medical advice is shaped both by outdated training and by the doctor's guess about your willpower. If you seem unlikely to change your lifestyle, the default is medication.
stories.quote: He looked a little embarrassed because at that moment I sensed that he knows that everything he has been taught is wrong and is pointless, but he can't say so. So he said, You're a smart man, you know what to do.

stories.topic: The friend who swore by oats
stories.summary: A friend kept insisting oats were healthy and called Amit crazy whenever he cited books and studies against them. Then she wore a CGM. Oats sent her glucose to 280, and eggs the next day left a flat line. She wore it for about a month, changed her lifestyle, and lost 25 kg.
stories.insight: Arguments rarely beat conventional wisdom, but seeing your own body's response does. Personal data persuaded her where citations could not.
stories.quote: She'd put the CGM, had oats, two eighty. Next day had eggs, flatlined.

stories.summary: While hiking in the hills near Dharamshala, Ajay reached a summit and had a 500 ml bottle of Gatorade, white rice and rajma. He then descended 1,000 metres while wearing a CGM. Normally such a meal produces one blurry, prolonged rise. Because he was burning energy so fast, he instead saw three distinct spikes, each burned off in turn. The Gatorade sugar came first, then the white rice as amylase converted it, and last the rajma's complex carbs.
stories.insight: Everyday life smears overlapping signals together and hides cause and effect. Under the right conditions, here an empty stomach and heavy exertion, the textbook account of how fast different carbs reach the blood becomes clearly visible.
stories.quote: I got to see something that I felt we don't see in our ordinary life. I saw three distinct surges.

stories.topic: Chess rating as a brain-fog meter
stories.summary: Amit plays bullet chess on chess.com under a pseudonym as an addict, not to improve, so his rating stays at a stable baseline. On keto it climbs about 150 points. After a cheat day with pizza it drops about 150, and more if he adds a biryani.
stories.insight: Sugar's cost to clear thinking is real and can be measured. Any consistent daily activity can serve as a personal gauge of how well your mind is working.
stories.quote: If I get off keto, have a cheat day, indulge on a pizza, it comes down one fifty points, or even more if I add a biryani to the pizza.

recommendations.item: The Case Against Sugar
recommendations.creator: Gary Taubes
recommendations.context: The key book among the four Amit asks every viewer to read. He reads its mission statement aloud.
recommendations.reason: In Amit's view it gives the best overarching account of the subject. It argues that sugar causes diabetes and obesity in the same causal sense that smoking causes lung cancer, through its hormonal effects rather than overeating. It is also the source of the Camel-cigarette history.

recommendations.item: The Big Fat Surprise
recommendations.creator: Nina Teicholz
recommendations.context: One of Amit's four essential books, called excellent and the source of the Kritchevsky quote and the obesity-epidemic chart.
recommendations.reason: It shows how the low-fat dogma and the Ancel Keys era misled a generation, and how dissenters were silenced.

recommendations.item: The Obesity Code
recommendations.creator: Jason Fung
recommendations.context: One of Amit's four essential books on sugar and nutrition.
recommendations.reason: Part of the core reading that convinced Amit that the standard dietary wisdom on weight is wrong.

recommendations.item: The Diabetes Code
recommendations.creator: Jason Fung
recommendations.context: Amit has gifted it to friends, who raved about it, and says it played a part in his own journey.
recommendations.reason: It lays out how type 2 diabetes can be reversed through diet, which is the premise of the whole episode.

recommendations.item: Sweetness and Power
recommendations.creator: Sidney Mintz
recommendations.context: The first of Amit's four must-read books. He quotes it on refined sucrose's 'peculiar physiological effects'.
recommendations.reason: It provides the historical grounding for understanding sugar's hold on us.

recommendations.item: The Botany of Desire
recommendations.creator: Michael Pollan
recommendations.context: Amit reads Pollan's account of his son Isaac's first taste of cake icing.
recommendations.reason: It captures, better than any statistic, how intoxicating and addictive sugar is from the very first taste.

recommendations.item: Nina Teicholz on The Joe Rogan Experience
recommendations.creator: Joe Rogan, Nina Teicholz
recommendations.context: Amit notes that Teicholz appeared on Rogan's show and promises a link.
recommendations.reason: An accessible entry point to Teicholz's case for readers not ready for the book.

recommendations.item: The perfect treatment for diabetes and weight loss (Jason Fung interviewed by Diet Doctor)
recommendations.creator: Jason Fung
recommendations.context: Linked while Amit attacks the dietitian advice that small, frequent meals are good.
recommendations.reason: It explains why frequent eating means frequent insulin spikes and moves you toward insulin resistance.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Brought up when Ajay asks whether rising sugar consumption is simply a matter of prosperity.
recommendations.reason: A 'great TIL' conversation that reframes diabetes and the ghunghat as markers of Dalit mobility and choice.

recommendations.item: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Cited for the phrase 'aggressively conventional minded', one of the sources of resistance to the new nutrition science.
recommendations.reason: It explains why some people defend received wisdom even when the evidence has moved on.

recommendations.item: Ajay speaks out against Hydroponics
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to his earlier discussion of hydroponics to explain the gut microbiome.
recommendations.reason: Plants fed simple fertilisers starve their root microbiome, and the same pattern explains what simple carbs do to the human gut.

recommendations.item: Host-diet-gut microbiome interactions influence human energy balance
recommendations.creator: Karen D Corbin et al.
recommendations.context: A June 2023 Nature Communications study that Ajay walks through in detail.
recommendations.reason: It compared diets with identical calories and found that complex carbs feed the gut microbiome, which consumes some of the energy. The result is roughly a 200-calorie-a-day 'discount', evidence that a calorie is not a calorie.

recommendations.item: Are all calories created equal? Your gut microbes don't think so.
recommendations.creator: Anahad O'Connor
recommendations.context: A show-notes link accompanying Ajay's discussion of the Corbin et al. study.
recommendations.reason: A readable newspaper account (Washington Post) of the gut-microbiome calorie findings.

recommendations.item: FreeStyle Libre Glucose Monitoring System (Reader & Sensor)
recommendations.creator: Abbott Labs
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the week. He was wearing one on his arm during the episode.
recommendations.reason: It is the CGM that made this whole journey possible. Ajay's tips: insert it and wait a full 24 hours before initialising for better accuracy, and expect it to differ from finger-prick readings because it tracks the average of the last 5-15 minutes. Amit's tips: calibrate with prick tests for a couple of days, and buy it directly, since services like Ultrahuman use the same sensor. Ajay also asks Abbott to open the API so readings can flow into a Google Sheet.

recommendations.item: Shruti Jahagirdar (nutritionist and physical trainer)
recommendations.context: Amit credits her, alongside Ajay, for his journey. Her contact details are in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: She designs a complete plan around your body weight and goals, advises vegetarians on keto, and believes in resistance training. She also taught Amit to skip multivitamins and take specific supplements such as B12, E and C.

recommendations.item: Shruti Jahagirdar is the Sporty One (Episode 289 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Shruti Jahagirdar
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the episode in which Shruti appeared.
recommendations.reason: A way to get to know her approach before consulting her.

recommendations.item: The Emergency: A Personal History
recommendations.creator: Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation for the week. Kapoor is a journalist who lived through those years, and her husband was jailed.
recommendations.reason: Too few people know this history. It shows how horrible the Emergency was, with half the opposition and hordes of journalists jailed, and why democracy must not be taken for granted.

recommendations.item: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: Amit mentions that Kapoor was on his show a few months earlier.
recommendations.reason: A companion conversation to her book, with someone Amit calls a 'really fine lady'.

recommendations.item: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (Episode 103 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Gyan Prakash
recommendations.context: Raised while arguing that the Emergency was not an aberration. Prakash has written another great book on it.
recommendations.reason: It frames the Emergency as part of the Indian state's centralising DNA, inherited from the colonial state.

recommendations.item: Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
recommendations.creator: David Remnick
recommendations.context: Ajay's book recommendation for the week, on the dying days of the USSR.
recommendations.reason: It shows how a society struggles with an authoritarian state and how progress is damaged for a very long time. It is doubly interesting now because we know what Remnick didn't: Russia was headed back to hell under Putin.

recommendations.item: The Bridge: The Life and Rise of Barack Obama
recommendations.creator: David Remnick
recommendations.context: Amit praises Remnick as one of the great journalists of our time and calls this a great book.
recommendations.reason: Full of revealing detail, including the trivia that Obama played poker to network with Democratic Party insiders.

recommendations.item: Louie
recommendations.creator: Louis CK
recommendations.context: Cited for Louis CK's routine about the 'bang bang'.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great show, and the bit perfectly names his pizza-plus-biryani binges.

core_ideas.concept: Sugar causes disease through hormones, not just overeating
core_ideas.explanation: Taubes's argument is that sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup cause obesity and diabetes in the same causal sense that cigarettes cause lung cancer. The cause is their distinct metabolic and hormonal effects, and the damage builds over decades, possibly passing to the next generation through the womb. Amit links sugar to hypertension, heart disease and possibly cancer, and notes that some researchers call Alzheimer's 'type 3 diabetes'.
core_ideas.quote: It is not because we eat too much of these sugars, although that is implied merely by the terms over consumption and overeating, but because they have unique physiological, metabolic and endocrinological, that is hormonal effects in the human body that directly trigger these disorders.

core_ideas.concept: The addiction we never notice
core_ideas.explanation: Sugar acts on the brain's reward centre the way nicotine and alcohol do. Unlike coffee, which makes you jittery, it gives no warning when you've had too much. And since we are almost never without it, we never feel withdrawal and so never realise we are hooked.
core_ideas.quote: We don't realize we are addicted. You know, we will never experience a withdrawal symptom because we are never without sugar for long enough to experience that withdrawal symptom.

core_ideas.concept: Nutrition science lags medicine
core_ideas.explanation: A consensus in medicine today is broadly reliable, but nutrition has stood on uncertain ground for a century. Its history includes siloed experts, industry-funded studies and dogmas, such as 'fat causes heart disease' and 'obesity is just calories in versus calories out', that hardened into official guidelines.
core_ideas.quote: In nutrition we have been on uncertain ground for a long, long time, as this narrative will show.

core_ideas.concept: Three forces keeping the old dogma alive
core_ideas.explanation: The first is corporate interest: processed foods hide sugar behind labels like 'no added sugar' and ingredients like concentrated apple juice. The second is Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional minded'. The third is self-interested defenders of the status quo, including doctors trained on outdated science. Amit warns that in India, a doctor over forty is likely to give bad advice unless they have kept updating themselves.
core_ideas.quote: If you've studied medicine, if you've studied nutrition, if you've studied in a particular way, chances are if you graduated in 2010 or even a little later, chances are you're wrong. The science has moved on.

core_ideas.concept: Type 2 diabetes is reversible
core_ideas.explanation: Amit is emphatic that type 2 diabetes is a disease of the diet, not a life sentence. His own HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7 through keto and fasting.
core_ideas.quote: It is reversible, type 2 diabetes, it can be reversed through diet alone. It is a disease of the diet.

core_ideas.concept: Every meal is an insulin spike, so eat less often
core_ideas.explanation: Every time you eat, insulin rises, and frequent spikes push you toward insulin resistance and eventually diabetes. That makes 'small frequent meals' bad advice and intermittent fasting a strong lifestyle. Amit suggests that is why fasting shows up in every major religion.
core_ideas.quote: Every time you eat something, there is an insulin spike. The more insulin spikes there are, the closer you're getting to insulin resistance, which is eventually going to give you diabetes.

core_ideas.concept: Eat the egg yolk
core_ideas.explanation: Cholesterol in food is not the cholesterol in your blood. Amit calls the yolk perhaps the healthiest food known to man, and points to Time magazine covers that swung from 'cholesterol is bad' to 'butter is good'.
core_ideas.quote: Dietary cholesterol has absolutely nothing to do with the cholesterol in our body.

core_ideas.concept: Know thyself: adapt your diet rather than adopt one
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay reframes the goal. Instead of following someone's book, start from your own tastes and food culture and adjust them until they work for your body. Tools like the CGM make this do-it-yourself approach possible, because different people really are different.
core_ideas.quote: In the world of diet, we are normally told, here's a diet. Whereas what we should be asking is where are my preferences? And what are my tastes and what is my food culture?

core_ideas.concept: Time in range beats a three-month average
core_ideas.explanation: HbA1c smears three months of blood sugar into one weighted average. A CGM shows the moment-by-moment pattern, so you can watch for surges and volatility. Ajay's target is to stay between 70 and 160 for over 80% of the day, never going below 70.
core_ideas.quote: A good thumb rule to aim for is that we should try to stay between 70 and 160 for over 80 percent of the day.

core_ideas.concept: Eating order matters
core_ideas.explanation: Carbs on an empty stomach hit the blood fast, the way alcohol does. Eating fibre first, then protein and fat, then carbs slows absorption, so the classic Western meal of salad, main course, then dessert turns out to be ideal. A 20-minute walk after a meal also blunts the spike.
core_ideas.quote: Starting with fiber is great. Having the protein second is perfect. Having the carbs last is great.

core_ideas.concept: Sugar is not just sugar; it matters what it comes with
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay tested the same dose of sugar three ways: alone, with fat, and with fat plus spices such as ginger, nutmeg and cinnamon. Each produced a visibly different surge. If you must have sugar, ice cream at the end of a meal, ideally spiced, is the least bad option.
core_ideas.quote: Sugar is not sugar, it matters what it goes with.

core_ideas.concept: White rice and maida are polymerised sugar
core_ideas.explanation: Simple starches are one enzyme reaction, via amylase, away from sugar, so 100 g of white rice is not much better than 100 g of sugar. We have simply normalised them. Ajay says whole grains, dals and skins slow things down, and that oats vary with how heavily processed they are. Amit counters that ultimately all carbs are sugar at some level.
core_ideas.quote: These simple starches, the white flour and the white rice, are merely polymerized sugars and they are one reaction away from becoming sugar.

core_ideas.concept: Treat the CGM as an annual habit-building project
core_ideas.explanation: CGMs are expensive, but you don't need one all the time. Behavioural economics suggests habits form over two to three months. So run a rigorous two-to-three-month experiment on yourself each year, then live on the habits it builds.
core_ideas.quote: Every year do two three rigorous months of CGM and that research project on ourselves.

core_ideas.concept: Food is social, so change what you buy
core_ideas.explanation: Willpower usually loses to whatever is easy to reach, so change has to happen at the point of purchase. That means talking to the family and friends you eat with. Ajay says it is fine, even advisable, to be 'rude' about eating differently.
core_ideas.quote: If there is cheesecake in the fridge, most of the time it's going to end up inside you. So you have to stop it at the root cause.

core_ideas.concept: A calorie is not a calorie
core_ideas.explanation: Calorie counts come from burning food in pure oxygen, which is not how the body processes it. Taubes argues carb calories drive insulin and fat storage differently from fat calories. The 2023 Corbin et al. study showed that complex carbs reach and feed the gut microbiome, with some measures 8x higher, and the microbes consume part of the energy. That amounted to roughly 200 calories a day of difference on identical-calorie diets.
core_ideas.quote: A calorie is not a calorie. By eating that same calorie in the form of complex carbs, we actually get a discount in terms of the calorific burden imposed on the human body because those blokes in the gut microbiome, they're eating some of it.

core_ideas.concept: The hydroponics parallel: starving your microbiome
core_ideas.explanation: Plants fed simple chemical fertiliser underinvest in their root microbiome and lose nutritional quality and disease resistance. Simple carbs do the same to humans: they are absorbed before reaching the gut, so the microbiome shrivels. Complex carbs travel all the way down and feed it.
core_ideas.quote: When we eat the sugars and the simple starches, very rapidly after the stomach, these things are absorbed into the body. Okay, so you get the sugar surge like we've been describing, but also the nutrition does not reach the gut microbiome.

core_ideas.concept: Doctors as amateur psychologists
core_ideas.explanation: For lifestyle diseases, doctors read your character and discipline and tailor their advice to what they think you will actually do. If they doubt you will change your lifestyle, they default to drugs.
core_ideas.quote: If they think that you're really not going to be able to execute lifestyle changes, they figure that I'm just going to drug the hell out of you.

core_ideas.concept: The invisible spillovers that markets don't capture
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's answer to the 'you made people cry' charge. Markets run on contracts and the 'double thank you' of a transaction, but much of what matters, like mentorship and influence, flows as unpriced positive or negative externalities between people.
core_ideas.quote: The most interesting stuff in life is just the invisible spillovers that are not intermediated by the market system.

core_ideas.concept: Read nutrition studies sceptically
core_ideas.explanation: Check who funded a study, since the sugar lobby is still powerful, and examine its methodology, starting from a critical default. Trust meta-studies over single studies. Applying this to the claim that a glass of wine is good for the heart, Amit asks what it does to the liver, and Ajay adds that studies show the best amount of alcohol is zero.
core_ideas.quote: Look at each study with a default position of being critical of it and then figuring out what's going on there.

core_ideas.concept: Multivitamins are a five-star buffet
core_ideas.explanation: Shruti Jahagirdar's advice, via Amit. Multivitamins give a little of everything but don't meet daily requirements, so work out exactly what you lack, especially on keto, and supplement that specifically.
core_ideas.quote: Multivitamins are horrible, kinda like a five-star buffet. That they'll have a little bit of a bunch of things but not meet your daily requirement.

core_ideas.concept: Ajay's ideas for the food industry
core_ideas.explanation: First, Indian sourdough makers should label clearly whether multigrain loaves are entirely whole grain. Second, a product idea: separate whole wheat into maida and the rest, remove about 10 units of the maida, and recombine. The result would be a superior atta with a built-in 10% discount on refined flour.
core_ideas.quote: So effectively I'm back to whole grain, which is atta, but I've got a discount because I've knocked out 10% of the maida. So this could be a superior atta.

core_ideas.concept: Democracy is not to be taken for granted
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that the Emergency was not an aberration. India's constitution centralised power enormously, and a dominant state is part of the Indian state's DNA, inherited from the colonial state. Ajay's matching point from Lenin's Tomb is that the rule of law and democratic culture take a very long time to build and are easily damaged.
core_ideas.quote: It's important to kind of recognize what a horrible time we went through, that our democracy is something we should not take for granted. We are lucky we came out of it. We have to keep fighting for it every day.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The naming joke that opens the show: 'We just thought that we could call this show Amit and Shah. Because you know, Amit and Shah. But we're not gonna do that.' (The pun is on a prominent politician's name.)

After Ajay answers the 'you made people cry' charge in economics-speak about externalities, Amit says: 'You know, I keep telling my writing students, don't use jargon, don't use jargon. Look what you just did.'

On Ajay's line that cheesecake in the fridge ends up inside you, Amit adds: 'If there is a choice of the cheesecake being inside you and you being inside the cheesecake, please choose the second option. Even if it is hard to imagine and a little bit messy and you'll need a good shower later. Midjourney, here we come... Ajay Shah inside a cheesecake.'

Ajay warns that concentrated apple juice is a standard way to sneak sugar into '100% fruit' products. Amit: 'I feel jealous of that kind of apple juice because I find it so hard to stay concentrated.'
Amit on rajma: 'Who doesn't love Rajma? Despite the windy things it does to you the next morning.'

Amit on doctors who call type 2 diabetes irreversible: 'any doctor who tells you type 2 diabetes is a chronic disease and cannot be reversed is a lying quack. Treat him as no better than a homeopathic doctor or an Ayurvedic doctor.'

Amit trips over his Obama trivia: 'Barack Obama was also just like me.' Ajay: 'A basketball player.' Amit: 'I'm not a basketball player. Barack Obama, just like me, was also a poker player.' He then weighs the trade-off: 'You avoid sugar but you get gambling. I don't know which is a bigger evil... I didn't get type two diabetes by playing poker, so we know what the answer to that is.'

The sign-off pitch: producer Vartika says Ajay needs patterned shirts, since he is down to the plain white ones he wears every day. So Ajay has been telling friends, 'guys, gift me shirts.' Amit: 'We want shirts, but like and subscribe.'
Michael Pollan once described Gary Taubes as 'a Solzhenitsyn of the nutrition world', for taking on nutrition orthodoxy.
Pollan in The Botany of Desire, on his son Isaac's first taste of birthday-cake icing, imagined as saying: 'Your world contains this. From this day onwards I shall dedicate my life to it.'

Kailas Chunder Bose, 1907: 'There is not the slightest shadow of a doubt that with the progress of civilization, of high education, and increased wealth and prosperity of the people under the British rule, the number of diabetic cases has enormously increased.'
Elliott Joslin's 1925 claim that automobiles cause diabetes, because people drive instead of walking, get fat and then get diabetes.
Franklin Roosevelt called the sugar lobby the most powerful interest group he had seen. Amit: 'This is a man who won World War II in a sense, but couldn't beat the sugar lobby.'
Time magazine covers trace the swing in nutrition wisdom, from 'cholesterol is bad news' to 'cholesterol is good news' to 'butter is good'.
Amit invokes The Insider, a film about the tobacco lobby, and calls what the sugar lobby did 'a far greater scandal'.

Louis CK's 'bang bang' from Louie: eat a complete meal at one restaurant, walk straight into another restaurant serving a different cuisine, and eat another complete meal. Amit's pizza-plus-biryani counts.
L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency: they were asked to bend, and they chose to crawl.
Ajay, recalling Gordon Brown: the rule of law is a difficult project for the first 500 years.
From David Remnick's The Bridge: Obama played poker in the late 1990s not for the game or the money, but because it was the best relaxed, alcohol-free way to network with Democratic Party insiders.
Amit closes with the ancient maxim 'know thyself', alongside 'sugar is poison', as the episode's two key messages.
